title: The Most Common Speaking Mistakes Teachers Make: Part 2 hers-make-part-2/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Continuing his series on teacher speech, Linsin addresses two more common mistakes: talking too much and repeating directions. He argues that excessive verbal support—caveats, background details, rambling—dilutes the core message and causes students to tune out or grow disruptive, so teachers should become 'discriminating with words' and focus only on the action students need to take. He similarly warns that habitually repeating directions removes any urgency for students to listen the first time, training them into passive, unresponsive listening. His fix is to give directions only once, only when students are fully quiet and attentive, which he claims transforms a class's listening habits within a short amount of time.
points: Excessive verbal support—caveats, warnings, background info, rambling—dilutes the core message and causes students to tune out or misbehave.
Students need only to know 'what they need to do or what they need to know'—not a running commentary of every why and what-if.
Habitually repeating directions removes urgency: if students know a direction will be repeated, there's no incentive to listen the first time.
Fix: give directions only once, and only when students are quiet and looking at the teacher, then hold them to it.
Cutting talking by a third and eliminating repetition frees up teacher time for observation and produces more precise, persuasive speech.
quotes: Most teachers talk too much—much more, in fact, than is necessary. Leaving no stone, slab, or tree stump unturned, they go on and on until their students have more information and encouragement than they’ll ever need.
When you provide too much verbal support, you dilute your message, confuse key points and critical information, and cause students to have to sift through the clutter.
Another common speaking mistake is the tendency to repeat the same directions more than once in succession—and sometimes three, four, and five times.
If your students know you’ll repeat yourself, then there is no urgency or responsibility to listen the first time—or any time.
Resolve to give directions only once—and only when your students are quiet and looking at you—and then expect them to be followed.
By cutting the amount of talking you do by a third, and committing to no longer repeating directions, your classroom will be transformed—no doubt about it.
